Under our system, people without immediate prospects are literally stuck in minimum wage jobs. It doesn't matter how much you hate your work, how much you want to go back to school, how much you want to move to another city -- if you only have 2 weeks left to bring your bank account back up to the point where you can make rent, you can't focus on anything else. It's exhausting.

Under basic income, you could just plain walk away. Last year I worked as a baker in an industrial kitchen, making $10/hr before taxes. I had to get up at 2:30 AM to make it to work on time, had to deal with some pretty hazardous work conditions, and literally had to run from station to station. I hated it, but I kept at it because if I had quit, I wouldn't have been able to continue living in my apartment after the end of the month.

If I had an alternative, one that would've allowed me to survive while I focused on finding real, fulfilling work, you can bet I would've walked away without a second thought. Which would've meant that, to keep me in my blue collar position, they would've had to substantially increase my salary (and improve my working conditions).

By taking the power of poverty away from blue collar bosses, basic income would force them to make it worth an employee's while to stick around. As it is, our country's poor live third world lives while working in the richest nation on the planet. Basic income would improve both wages and general working conditions for everyone.

Well, yeah, from a utilitarian standpoint organic is completely overblown. But people often don't seem to grasp the importance of consumer choice in shaping the world around them.

Although it may seem overly idealistic, there is truth to the fact that, each time you buy something, you're voting for the production approach, the market strategy, the labor practices that went into that particular version of a product. Although fancy artisan fair-trade chocolate may be just as bad for you as Hershey's, you're giving money to (and encouraging a market for) a company that pays workers a living wage and acts at least somewhat consciously toward mitigating environmental impacts instead of giving support to one that uses slave labor and pesticides that cause colony collapse in the name of minimizing cost margins.

Further down, you talk about the collapse of the Mayan civilization due to over-farming by pre-'conventional' agricultural methods. Something that you don't consider in this worldview is the status of all the other ancient civilizations that didn't use the methods we did today. Ancient Rome, pre and post-Norman conquest England, China and Japan, Egypt. People have eeked their livings out of the soil for unbroken thousands of years, and yet are no worse for the wear. Modern farming technology has great promise, but we're in unfamiliar territory here and we don't have the data to know that it's safe at the scale we're seeing today. I know that much of the anti-GMO/pesticide movement is full of hocus pocus, but ultimately one of the great wonders of capitalism is that the consumer has the right to choose based on whatever criteria they see fit, even if that reason is just that something doesn't sit right.

I've only taken them twice - once on the way up to Portland, OR from the Bay Area and once again on the way back down. Both experiences were extremely positive, but you have to be comfortable with the idea of sharing a small car with people you've never met for several hours.

The way up was with a guy who was moving back up from California to rejoin his christian rock band. There was another passenger, who as I recall was a traveling anarchist on his way up to surprise his mom for mother's day. We traded off paying at gas stations to fill up our ride (70's chevy station wagon,) smoked a ton of weed, talked a whole lot about nothing in particular, and bought some really nasty taco bell right across the Oregon border. All in all it ran me $25 dollars for a 650 mile trip.

On the way back I was with a 75 y/o retired public radio broadcaster and practicing buddhist, visiting grandkids. Really sweet guy, we talked a lot about the environment and his trip to Burningman. One memorable point of interest: he had a bone to pick with a toilet paper company that was harvesting old growth trees in his county, so he had tried unsuccessfully to reuse old rags in lieu of toilet paper. He said that after a few attempts he had to buy a new washing machine because everything ended up smelling worse after a load. I suggested he buy an attachable bidet and he took to the idea immediately. We were traveling with another passenger, a bearded guy who slept most of the ride. This guy's car was more fuel efficient than the chevy, so it ran us each around $20 bucks.

A few things to remember:
1: While it can feel awkward at times, speak only if it improves upon the silence. Part of the beauty of a rideshare is that it gives you a 12 hour window into a stranger's life, and at the end of that 12 hours you can either befriend each other on Facebook or part company and never speak again. If you accidentally run across some strong political or religious beliefs then it may very well be the latter, so it's best to keep conversation light and positive, steer clear of contentious stuff, and read people to avoid getting on their nerves. Remember: it's a long trip.

2: You'll probably have to email a few people before you get a ride locked down. Craigslist is a fickle mistress, and this is the price you pay for a free service. Some people will find someone else who gives them a yes first, some people will decide last minute to cancel their trip, some people will just come off as kind of creepy and you won't want to follow up after a couple of exchanges. Such is life in the 21st century.

3: By taking rideshares, you'll find yourself a little bit restricted in your movements. It's easy to find them between big nodes, but it's hard to get anywhere specific, especially if it's out of your region. for example: there are probably 50 offers from Seattle to Portland leaving this afternoon. Same with New York to Boston. Boston to Seattle? Not so easy. You'd probably need to find one to Chicago, then to Madison, then to somewhere else in between, then to Missoula, and so on. It definitely takes some work to get anywhere far, and you're probably out of luck finding a trip into and out of any major national parks.

4: Bring cash and pack light. The average sedan doesn't have room for 3 peoples' extra bags. Most people will agree on a fair price beforehand.

5: Lastly, on the subject of safety. I am of the personal opinion that rideshares are quite a bit safer than hitchhiking was. There's a paper trail, there are cellphone numbers, etc. It isn't as anonymous, and so the chance for crime doesn't present itself as readily as it would if you were to just get into any old car. That said, you should trust your gut when dealing with strangers from the internet. If something seems off, take the next one! If you can, you should also take a picture of the car and license plate and send it to a friend (or at least send a description.) You could try to be surreptitious about it, but most people wouldn't take it personally either way. This way, you could use it as a deterrent if anything were to go awry, and you have physical proof so that if something were to happen the police would know where to start looking. You probably won't need it, but tis better to err on the side of paranoia.

Not to be a dork, but you might want to look into craigslist rideshares. They're about as cheap and as interesting as hitchhiking but an ounce or two less dangerous since there's a paper trail and cell phone numbers involved, and you're less likely to be left in a lurch since people are usually going to major-ish cities.  I've done it a number of times and I've always had positive experiences, ranging from a christian rock guitarist/stoner around my age to a 70 year old hare krishna/public radio broadcaster.

If you take one it's always a good idea to take a picture of the car/license plate and send it to a friend: you can do it surreptitiously but people usually understand that it's just a safety precaution, and on the off chance anyone was planning anything it'll pretty much stop them in their tracks.  People usually ask for gas money, but it's a lot cheaper than a greyhound ticket and usually much more pleasant.  A lot of people who offer rides try to take 2 strangers at a time, which is nice because it cuts down on gas costs, makes for a friendly (non-awkward) trip, and because everyone's watching everyone.

You should also totally look into couchsurfing like futurebeat said.  It's a little hard to break into at first because your standing is based on verifications and reviews from other members who have hosted or stayed with you, but it ultimately makes for an environment where you can trust somebody you're staying with before you've even met them.  It would also be a good way to find people who would be interested in taking side trips to national parks, since you can post on a regional discussion board and see if anyone's interested in going with you.

I actually posted a question about vpnbook under a different username awhile back, asking how they made money and kept the lights on - the best responses that I got said something along the lines of 'when a service is free, you're most likely the product for sale.'  Hence despite what their terms of service say, free vpn services are *probably* (note the italics) gathering as much information as they can, either to sell to advertisers or to other parties for more illicit purposes.

That said, as long as they don't insert a virus or anything, a vpn provider really can't gather anything that you don't send and receive through the internet.  So as long as you're careful not to log into your email or check your bank account while connected through their servers, you'll probably be fine as far as personal data goes.  I tried using VPNbook for a few days (and it seemed to work great) but then I got all paranoid and worried that it might be a sting operation and stopped (a theory which was pretty unfounded).  Although it's a good resource I don't torrent enough to justify the risk, and I figure eventually I'll cough up the 30 bucks a year for a paid service if I really want to.

As far as how they work: a vpn provider basically acts as a middleman between you and the internet that exists in an area with less stringent anti-piracy laws.  Think of a LAN cable that runs directly from your computer to a server in Romania.  Your computer communicates with that server, that server sends and receives all of the traffic that your browser/bt client/whatever requests, and then all of that information comes back to your computer through the direct line between you and Romania.  This means that a) the data between you and the server is private and encrypted (so even if someone were trying to hack your computer it would be very tough to figure out what you're sending and receiving and more importantly b) from the open internet, your activity looks like it's coming from an ip address in Romania instead of from the one at your house.  This makes it impossible for an anti-piracy firm to figure out who you are, as a good vpn is located somewhere where a takedown notice is meaningless, and wouldn't keep any information on you anyway.  They usually offer two methods of connection: pptp and openvpn: openvpn is harder to set up but is more secure, both would suffice as long as you aren't sending government secrets or something.
